questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: Verb position in the main clause
questions.learningObjective: place the finite verb in second position after a fronted time expression
questions.stem: A student must order the pieces 'Am Montag', 'ich', 'habe', 'einen freien Tag'. Which arrangement is the one a speaker would accept?

options.text: Am Montag habe ich einen freien Tag, because the verb comes second
Am Montag ich habe einen freien Tag, because the subject fills position one
options.misconception: believes the subject must stay in the first slot after a fronted time word

options.text: Ich habe am Montag einen freien Tag, because a time may not lead here
options.misconception: thinks a time expression is forbidden in the first position

options.text: Am Montag einen freien Tag ich habe, because the object can lead too
options.misconception: believes the object can open the clause ahead of the finite verb

questions.explanation: In a German main clause the conjugated verb stands in the second position, and only one element may claim the first. Am Montag is a time expression, so it takes that slot and pushes the finite verb into position two, which leaves the gap after the verb for the subject ich and then the object. The reason the rule matters is that the first position is not reserved for the subject: a subject-first clause such as Ich habe am Montag einen freien Tag is equally correct, because there the subject fills position one. The error the learner should watch for is treating position one as a permanent home for the subject.
questions.hint: Ask which single element the writer wants to put in front of everything else.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: Verb position in the main clause
questions.learningObjective: recognise that a question word also counts as position one
questions.stem: Two colleagues argue about 'Wo bleibt die Karte?' and 'Die Karte bleibt auf dem Tisch.' What settles where the finite verb goes in each?

options.text: Question word and subject each count as position one, so the verb follows
Only a subject counts as position one, so the question word stays behind
options.misconception: believes a question word has no place in the first position

options.text: A question sends the verb to the end, and only a statement uses position two
options.misconception: assumes questions in German are always verb-final

options.text: Both sentences are verb-final, since German never counts what stands first
options.misconception: thinks the language has no first-position rule at all

questions.explanation: The same rule covers both sentences. In Wo bleibt die Karte? the question word wo occupies position one, so the finite verb bleibt comes second and the subject die Karte follows it; if the subject came first instead, the question would be Die Karte bleibt wo and sound inverted. In the statement Die Karte bleibt auf dem Tisch the subject fills position one and the verb bleibt still sits in position two. The trap is the impression that a question pushes the verb to the end, which is true in English and in French but not in German.
questions.hint: Count the elements standing before the verb in each sentence.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.learningObjective: place a detached prefix at the end of the clause
questions.stem: A learner types 'Am Montag stehe ich früh auf' and a classmate says the word order is wrong. Which account of aufstehen is right?

options.text: Auf is separable, so it leaves the verb and closes the clause at the end
Auf is inseparable, so it must stay welded to the verb for ever
options.misconception: believes a prefix that looks like a word part is always inseparable

options.text: Auf follows the subject, since every prefix stands right after its pronoun
options.misconception: places the prefix after the subject as a fixed slot

options.text: Auf belongs in the gap after stehe, in the space the subject leaves
options.misconception: puts the prefix inside the verb bracket instead of the clause end

questions.explanation: The prefix of aufstehen is separable, so in a main clause the finite part stehe stands in position two and the prefix auf is detached and placed at the very end: Am Montag stehe ich früh auf. Only the conjugated verb stehe counts as the second element; the prefix does not move into the gap. The opposite case is worth keeping in view, because der Auf, a noun meaning a start in sports, is written as one word with no detachment at all, and the verbs verstehen, verkaufen and bekommen are inseparable and keep their prefix attached while taking no ge- in the participle.
questions.hint: Ask which half of the verb is the conjugated one in a main clause.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.learningObjective: fill the gap a detached prefix leaves open
questions.stem: Someone builds 'Er steht am Sonntag um sieben Uhr auf' and asks why two time expressions sit inside the verb rather than after it. What justifies that?

options.text: Any elements may fill the gap, so both times stay between stehe and auf
Only one element can ever stand between the verb and its detached prefix
options.misconception: assumes the gap holds a single element and no more

options.text: Time expressions must follow the whole verb, prefix included, for clarity
options.misconception: believes time material is banned from the gap before the prefix

options.text: The gap is reserved for pronouns, and two time words belong behind auf
options.misconception: thinks only pronouns may stand between the verb and the prefix

questions.explanation: When a separable verb splits, the space between the two halves is free for any number of elements, which is why Er steht am Sonntag um sieben Uhr auf is idiomatic. Both time phrases belong to the act of getting up, so keeping them in the gap ties them to the verb; pushing them behind auf would produce a different focus rather than a repair. The rule a learner needs is positive, not a prohibition: the finite verb is second, the prefix is last, and everything else is free to sit in between.
questions.hint: Ask how many elements German allows between the two halves of a split verb.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.learningObjective: place the finite verb last after a subordinating conjunction
questions.stem: A sentence reads 'Wir fahren morgen nach Köln, weil ich Zeit habe.' Where does the conjugated verb stand inside the reason clause?

options.text: At the very end, because a clause opened by weil puts its verb last
In second position, because a clause follows the rule of the main clause
options.misconception: carries the main-clause verb rule into a weil-clause

options.text: Directly after weil, because the conjunction hands the verb its place
options.misconception: believes the conjunction itself counts as position one in the clause

options.text: Before the subject ich, because pronouns tend to follow the verb in German
options.misconception: puts a pronoun subject ahead of the verb in a subordinate clause

questions.explanation: weil is a subordinating conjunction, and everything it introduces is a subordinate clause, so the conjugated verb goes to the very end: weil ich Zeit habe. The conjunction itself sits in position zero and is not counted, which is why the subject ich stands directly after weil. Two halves in one sentence therefore behave differently: the main clause keeps the verb in second position and the reason clause keeps it last, and a learner who expects one rule everywhere is surprised by the second half.
questions.hint: Ask whether weil opens a clause that can stand on its own as a statement.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.learningObjective: use a fronted subordinate clause as position one of the main clause
questions.stem: A student rewrites 'Dass es regnet, weiß ich' as '..., ich weiß' and asks whether the new order is allowed. What is the answer?

options.text: Yes, the fronted dass-clause is position one, so weiß still comes second
No, a dass-clause can never open a sentence in German
options.misconception: believes a subordinate clause is barred from the first position

options.text: Yes, but the verb then has to move to the end, since the clause leads
options.misconception: thinks a fronted clause drags the main verb into final position

options.text: No, only a prepositional phrase may stand in the first position
options.misconception: restricts position one to prepositional phrases only

questions.explanation: Dass es regnet, weiß ich is a fixed everyday pattern: the dass-clause is pushed to the front and occupies the first position of the main clause, and the finite verb of the main clause, weiß, stays in position two with its subject after it. Nothing about the leading clause changes the main clause's internal order. The pattern also works with other subordinating conjunctions, as in Weil es regnet, bleibe ich zu Hause, and with fronted adverbials such as Heute bleibe ich zu Hause.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.learningObjective: identify the auxiliary and the final participle in a perfect sentence
questions.stem: A shopkeeper's note reads 'Ich habe den Rekord noch nicht bezahlt.' Which part of the sentence carries the past-into-present meaning?

options.text: The present-tense form habe, since a perfect places the event before now
The participle bezahlt, since only a participle can carry tense at all
options.misconception: believes the participle alone supplies the tense of a perfect

options.text: The word noch, because it converts a present action into a finished one
options.misconception: reads the intensifier noch as a tense marker of its own

options.text: The word nicht, because a negative makes an action count as over
options.misconception: believes negation performs the work of the auxiliary

questions.explanation: A perfect is built from a present-tense form of haben or sein in position two and a Partizip II at the end of the clause, so Ich habe den Rekord noch nicht bezahlt is assembled as auxiliary, subject, object, negation, participle. The auxiliary is what links the event to the present, while the participle names the process, so noch and nicht slot in before it. The structural point worth memorising is that the participle closes the clause and never stands directly after the auxiliary, which is the error a learner makes when writing hat bezahlt den Rekord.
questions.hint: Ask which word is the conjugated helper and which word closes the clause.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.learningObjective: choose sein for a verb of motion from one place to another
questions.stem: A traveller says 'Gestern bin ich mit dem Zug nach Leipzig gefahren.' Why has the writer chosen sein rather than haben?

options.text: The sentence reports a change of place, which is sein's work in a perfect
The sentence reports a spoken claim, so sein is the verb of saying
options.misconception: believes sein is the auxiliary for any report about words

options.text: The sentence reports a lasting property of the traveller, not one event
options.misconception: reads a single completed journey as a permanent trait

options.text: The sentence reports a ticket, so sein is used whenever money appears
options.misconception: links the choice of auxiliary to the presence of a purchase

questions.explanation: German builds the perfect of verbs of motion from one place to another, and of change of state, with sein rather than haben, so fahren takes sein: Ich bin nach Leipzig gefahren. The clearest contrast is the pair Ich bin in den Bus gestiegen against Ich habe den Bus verpasst, where the first reports movement and the second reports a non-arrival. Learners who hear English have no reason to distinguish the two auxiliaries at all, which is why Ich habe gefahren is such a common guess, even though a perfect with habe is perfectly normal for verbs without motion, as in Ich habe lange gearbeitet.
questions.hint: Ask whether the subject ended up somewhere different from where it started.

questions.learningObjective: choose sein for a reported change of state
questions.stem: A news bulletin reads 'Die Preise sind im Sommer stark gestiegen.' What makes sein the auxiliary the writer needs here?

options.text: The clause reports a change of state, one of sein's perfect-verb uses
The clause names an object, and sein is the only verb that can take one

options.text: The clause reports a length of time, so sein marks anything that lasts
options.misconception: thinks duration alone decides between the two auxiliaries

options.text: The clause names a speaker, so sein is used whenever a person appears
options.misconception: ties the auxiliary to the presence of a human subject

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.learningObjective: recognise the -en participle of a weak verb
questions.stem: A drill lists three participles: gemacht, gelernt and gesagt. What do the three endings tell you about their verbs?

options.text: The verbs are weak and form the participle with ge- and the ending -en
The verbs are strong and change the stem vowel when the participle is built
options.misconception: reads an -en participle as the mark of a vowel change

options.text: The verbs take no ge- at all, because weak verbs never carry a prefix
options.misconception: believes the ge- prefix belongs only to strong verbs

options.text: The verbs end in -en, so the participle is the infinitive with nothing added
options.misconception: believes the ending -en is just the infinitive showing through

questions.explanation: machen, lernen and sagen are weak verbs, and a weak verb normally forms its Partizip II with ge- plus the stem plus an ending of -en or -t, with no change of the stem vowel. These three take -en: gemacht, gelernt, gesagt, and the same verbs in the simple past add -te to the stem, as in lernte. A second group of weak verbs takes -t instead, as in gekauft, gearbeitet and gewartet, and the two groups are best learned together so that the pattern rather than the individual verb is what travels.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.learningObjective: handle weak verbs in -ieren, which drop the ge- prefix
questions.stem: A learner must fill a table with bestellt, geöffnet and studiert. Which statement fits all three forms at once?

options.text: All are weak, but the -ieren verb forms its participle without the ge-
All are strong, since a weak verb must also change the stem vowel here
options.misconception: believes the -t ending proves a strong verb in every case

options.text: All are strong, since the ge- prefix appears only on strong participles
options.misconception: inverts the rule and treats ge- as a marker of strong verbs

options.text: All are weak, and the missing ge- in studiert is a spelling mistake
options.misconception: reads a regular rule about -ieren as an orthographic error

questions.explanation: bestellen and öffnen are weak verbs with a normal participle: bestellt and geöffnet, both ge- plus stem plus -t. Verbs in -ieren behave differently, because the -ier- ending already marks them as verbs and the participle takes no ge-: studiert, telefoniert, fotografiert. A learner who writes gestudiert has applied the general weak pattern too literally, and one who writes studierte has written a simple past form where a participle was wanted. The exception is small but common enough in everyday vocabulary that it is worth learning as a group.
questions.hint: Ask which of the three verbs ends in -ieren and what that changes.

questions.learningObjective: give the correct present-tense ending for ihr
questions.stem: Two students fill the blank in 'Ihr ___ die ganze Zeit am Fenster gesessen.' Which ending does the pronoun ihr need?

options.text: seid, because ihr is the second person plural and takes the ending -d
sind, because every plural pronoun in German takes the same ending
options.misconception: assumes plural pronouns are all identical in the present tense

options.text: seid, because ihr takes exactly the same form as the polite Sie
options.misconception: believes the informal plural and the polite form are one pronoun

options.text: sind, because the participle in the sentence fixes the auxiliary for you
options.misconception: reads a participle as evidence for the form of the subject pronoun

questions.stem: A report needs last year in writing and a writer tries 'Letztes Jahr ich habe in Wien gearbeitet.' Which corrected version is idiomatic?

options.text: Letztes Jahr habe ich in Wien gearbeitet, the perfect used as the spoken past
Letztes Jahr war ich in Wien gearbeitet, a simple past built with the verb sein
options.misconception: pairs a simple-past auxiliary with a participle in one clause

questions.learningObjective: form the simple past of a modal verb
questions.stem: A speaker says 'Als Kind konnte ich nicht schwimmen' and a class asks for the simple past form of the modal verb. What is it?

options.text: konnte, because a modal takes the weak simple-past ending -te on its stem
konntest, because a modal agrees with the subject of its clause
options.misconception: picks the second person singular form for an ich subject

options.text: gekonnt, because modals form their past with a participle like all verbs
options.misconception: believes a modal builds a participle in the perfect

options.text: könne, because the simple past of a modal is built in the subjunctive
options.misconception: confuses the simple past with the second subjunctive

questions.learningObjective: tell a strong from a weak simple past by the stem

lernte is strong and keeps the stem, schrieb is weak and changes it

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.learningObjective: teach the two jobs of the German subjunctives
questions.stem: A teacher has told a class that German has two subjunctives, and a learner now mixes them in written work. Explain the difference in a form the learner can apply on the next exercise.

answer.exemplar: The two moods are chosen by who owns the claim. A report of what someone said takes the first subjunctive, built on the bare stem, so Der Trainer sagt, das Spiel sei hart uses sei from sein and seien for the plural, habe from haben, könne from können, and komme, nehme, gehe and sehe from the strong verbs. Anything the speaker imagines rather than reports takes the second: wishes, softened requests and unreal conditions, as in Wenn ich mehr Zeit hätte and Könntest du mir helfen. The question to ask before writing either one is whether the sentence is claiming what someone else said or describing a situation the writer treats as counterfactual, because writing a second-subjunctive form inside a report turns a quotation into speculation.

answer.exemplar: The auxiliary reports the subject's relation to the action, not the verb's shape. With haben the subject stays put and performs the activity, and with sein it arrives somewhere it was not, or ends up in a condition it was not in. So Ich bin nach Berlin gefahren takes sein for the change of place and Ich habe dort zwei Jahre gearbeitet takes haben for the period of activity. The same split carries the spoken past, where the present form of the auxiliary does the identical job, so Ich bin gefahren and Ich habe gearbeitet are both ordinary in conversation. The short question that settles nearly every case while writing is whether the subject is now somewhere else, or in a state it was not in before, and the verbs that resist the rule are best memorised as fixed pairs.

questions.stem: A learner knows that German adjectives change their endings but cannot say what decides the change. Explain the difference between the positions, using one adjective in each.

answer.exemplar: What stands in front of the adjective decides how much the adjective must say. After der, die or das the article already carries gender, number and case, so the adjective is weak: der neue Wagen, das neue Auto, den neuen Wagen, die neuen Wagen. After ein or kein the article says almost nothing, so the adjective is strong and takes the endings itself: ein neuer Wagen, eine neue Jacke, ein neues Auto, keine neuen Wagen. The third position catches most learners, because after a linking verb an adjective describes the subject and takes no ending at all: Der Wagen ist neu and Die Tür ist offen, never Der Wagen ist neuer or Die Tür ist offene. Asking what the word before the adjective is doing settles all three.

questions.learningObjective: teach comparative and superlative forms
questions.stem: A learner wants to report that one route is quicker, that a flat in the old town is the cheapest available, and that a film was the most successful of the year. Explain the three forms German needs.

answer.exemplar: Three forms are needed. Comparing two things takes the comparative, which adds -er and is introduced by als rather than by wie: Der direkte Weg ist schneller als der lange. Most comparatives also change the stem vowel, so alt gives älter, groß gives größer and jung gives jünger, while a small irregular group must be learned in pairs, with gut giving besser, viel giving mehr and hoch giving höher. A superlative in a sentence is built with am or beim plus the adjective plus -sten, as in Der Wagen ist am schnellsten, while in front of a noun it takes the definite article and the ending -ste, as in Der schnellste Wagen. The two recurring errors are reaching for wie after a comparative, which English allows and German does not, and leaving the Umlaut out of the common adjective families.

questions.stem: Stage one: state the case that an takes in 'Das Bild hängt an der Wand' and give the rule behind it. Stage two: rewrite the sentence so the picture is on its way to the wall.

answer.exemplar: Stage one: an is one of the nine two-way prepositions, and the sentence reports a position rather than a movement, so it takes the dative and the noun appears as an der Wand. Stage two: once the picture is being carried towards the wall the preposition takes the accusative and the verb changes from the intransitive hängen, which reports where something is, to the transitive hängen, which reports the act of putting it there, giving Ich hänge das Bild an die Wand. Swapping only the articles produces a sentence about a different event, and keeping the intransitive verb cannot express the movement at all, because the verb and the case are one decision.

questions.explanation: The case in the first sentence is the dative, because an is one of the nine two-way prepositions and the sentence reports a position rather than a movement, so the noun stands in the dative with its definite article. The second stage reverses the meaning, and with it the case: once the picture is being carried towards the wall the preposition takes the accusative, and the verb changes from the intransitive hängen to the transitive hängen, which reports the act of putting it there. A learner who swaps only the articles has produced a sentence about a different event, and one who keeps the intransitive verb cannot express the movement at all, because the verb choice and the case belong to the same decision.
questions.hint: Ask whether the picture is being moved or is already in place.
